what_it_does: Many AI applications need to find the most similar item in a giant list of stored descriptions — a process called approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS). Today this is typically done on a regular processor or graphics card, but both struggle because finding neighbors requires fetching huge amounts of data from memory chips (DRAM — the large, slow storage bank in a computer) and then sorting the results, which creates bottlenecks. This paper proposes SeIM, a chip design that moves the distance-calculation work down into the memory chips themselves (a technique called processing-in-memory, or PIM), so that the data never has to travel far to be processed. Sorting, which needs results from many memory units to be combined, is handled at a higher level called the memory controller, which can see data from all the units and applies a filtering trick to reduce how much information needs to be passed around. The result is a faster, more energy-efficient way to support AI applications — such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), where a language model looks up relevant facts before answering — that depend heavily on this kind of similarity search.
